articles.title: 📱 Phone Giant Finally Unveils Its First Folding Phone; The Future Has Arrived, Costs Considerably More, Does The Same Things, And Now Bends In Half
articles.dateline: CUPERTINO — reported from a very expensive crease
paras: The world's most famous phone maker took the stage today to unveil its long-rumored first folding phone — a sleek, hinged marvel that opens into a small tablet, folds back into a phone, and answers the one question everyone has been asking for years: what if your phone, but it bends?

"It's the most personal device we've ever made," the company said, of a phone that is largely the previous phone, now with a fold. Analysts hailed the engineering while noting the industry has reached a familiar milestone: after a decade of adding cameras and shaving millimeters, the great remaining frontier of human progress turned out to be a hinge. Early buyers report the fold is deeply satisfying, right up until they remember the price, at which point it becomes deeply satisfying again, just more slowly.

articles.title: 🤖 Humanoid Robots Enter Mass Production; The Factory Of Tomorrow Will Be Staffed By The Coworkers Of Tomorrow, Who Never Ask For A Raise
articles.dateline: THE ASSEMBLY LINE — reported beside a robot that was also reporting
paras: A carmaker announced it has begun mass-producing humanoid robots, with large-scale output expected by year's end — meaning the two-legged, human-shaped worker of science fiction is quietly moving from prototype demo to actual product you can, in principle, order by the pallet.

"They'll handle repetitive tasks," the company said, of a workforce that shows up early, never tires, and has no opinions about the break room. Sociologists note a certain circularity: humans spent centuries designing machines to avoid dull labor, and have now built a machine shaped exactly like a human to go do it, presumably so it feels more natural when it takes over your shift.

articles.title: 🏭 Nation Unveils Plan To Quadruple Its A.I. Computing Power By 2030; The Target Is A Number So Large No Human Can Actually Picture It
articles.dateline: THE FIVE-YEAR PLAN — reported in exaflops, whatever those are
paras: A major government unveiled an ambitious plan to more than quadruple its national A.I. computing capacity by the end of the decade, setting a target measured in "exaflops" — a unit so enormous it exists mainly to be announced in press releases and nodded at solemnly.

"This is a national priority," officials said, of a goal that amounts to building an unimaginable amount of computer, then building four times more. Experts note the global A.I. race has entered its arms-buildup phase, in which nations compete to accumulate raw computing the way empires once counted battleships — the key difference being that a battleship is at least a thing you can point at, whereas an exaflop is a feeling you have about a warehouse.

articles.title: 🙇 A.I. Chief Publicly Apologizes For A Rocky Launch; The Most Powerful Model On Earth Arrived And Then, Briefly, Buffered
articles.dateline: THE STATUS PAGE — reported between error messages
paras: The head of a leading A.I. lab issued a public apology to paying subscribers after the debut of its most advanced model yet turned bumpy — a rollout in which the most sophisticated machine intelligence ever created stumbled over the ancient, humbling problem of too many people trying to use it at once.

"We're sorry, and we're fixing it," the chief said, of a launch that proved even a superintelligence must first survive its own opening day. Experts note the reassuring lesson buried in the chaos: we have built a system smart enough to reason about nearly anything, and it can still be brought to its knees by the same thing that crushes concert-ticket websites — everybody wanting it at 10 a.m.

articles.title: 🔬 Chipmakers Upgrade A Component You've Never Heard Of From 6 Inches To 12; The Future Runs On Parts You Will Never Once See
articles.dateline: THE CLEANROOM — reported through three layers of protective suit
paras: The world's top chip-tool makers announced a joint effort to upgrade the "photomask" — a decades-old stencil used to etch circuits onto silicon — from a six-inch format to twelve, a change invisible to everyone on Earth except the roughly four hundred people who care about it enormously.

"It's a foundational shift," the companies said, of an improvement to a part that most humans will live and die without ever knowing existed. Analysts note the quiet truth of modern technology: beneath every dazzling folding phone and apologetic superintelligence lies a vast, unseen scaffolding of impossibly precise machinery, tended by specialists, measured in inches you'll never look at, making the future one microscopic stencil at a time.

horoscopes.text: You will fold something in half today and feel briefly like the future. Then you will unfold it. This, too, is the future.
A robot will start work near you this week. Be kind. It never asked to be shaped like you. Neither, honestly, did you.
Everyone wants the same thing at 10 a.m. So do you. Wait your turn. Even the superintelligence had to.

tech_tip: Before you buy the folding phone, sit with the price for a full minute. Before you panic about exaflops, remember you can't picture one anyway. The unseen photomask, meanwhile, is doing fine. Thank it silently.
gadget_watch: This week's gadget is a phone that now folds in half — the same phone, plus a hinge, minus a chunk of your savings. Also entering production: a human-shaped robot for your workplace. Your desk and your pocket are both getting upgrades you didn't request.
